For Japanese 1:150 N-scale layouts. Generates laser-cut SVG plans with tongue-and-slot joinery.
Building Type
Dimensions
Ground Floor
Settings that distinguish the ground floor from the upper floors. Use these for shopfronts, lobbies, factory loading levels, kura with stone bases, or sukiya-style covered walkways.
Real buildings often have a taller ground floor for shops, lobbies, or loading. All upper floors keep the standard floor height.
Useful for shop fronts, lobbies, or ground-level retail with larger or wider windows than the upper floors.
Common for kura (stone or namako-kabe base under white plaster upper), brick or stone bases under timber or render, retail facades with stone trim. Splits each wall's cladding into two panels.
Common in Japanese architecture: ground-floor shop projects forward of the upper-floor footprint, OR upper floors overhang the ground floor (covered walkway / arcade). Adds an extra sub-assembly on the front face. Positive value = extends forward; negative = recessed under upper-floor overhang.
Horizontal decorative strip glued where the first floor meets the second floor — common on commercial buildings, brick warehouses, and machiya. Notches automatically around any openings (windows that cross the floor line, etc.).
Defaults
Properties that control what gets placed by default. Each individual window, door, trim, etc. can still be overridden in the floor editor.
Roof
Which walls extend up as parapets to hide the gable peak behind. With FB or EW only, the gable's ridge runs perpendicular to the parapet wall so the parapets are on the peak-end sides; the other two walls show the roof slopes meeting their flat eave tops.
Four foldable cladding strips that wrap over the parapet wall top and continue down the inside face to the roof deck, hiding both the exposed top edge and the inner parapet face.
A single 3 mm-wide strip with an etched centre fold line, sized to the roof's ridge length. Score along the etch, fold to match the ridge angle, and glue 1.5 mm to each slope along the seam where the two roof panels meet.
How far the roof projects past the walls on every side. The cladding above will extend to cover the full overhang.
Front / back East / west
Flat cladding pieces sized to the underside of each eave overhang (one per eave side). Glue to the bottom of the overhang where it sticks out past the wall — covers the otherwise-bare core material visible from below. Sized to the overhang's slope distance for gabled roofs (so it covers the full sloped underside).
3 mm-wide trim strips that follow the roof's perimeter, hiding the exposed core material at the panel edges. Gabled: a chevron piece outlining each gable peak's V-shape (the "triangle on each gable") plus a straight strip along each eave (the "end cap"). Slanted: a parallelogram per slanted-top wall, with vertical short ends so the wall's top edge looks flat-finished rather than tapering inward to a thin point.
Cladding Style
A second cladding panel per wall, glued to the inside face. Doors and windows are cut at the same wall positions so each opening lines up with the matching hole in the exterior cladding and the wall core. Independent style — pick a smooth interior finish even when the exterior is something textured.
Windows
Doors
Doors are placed at ground level. Walls with bay openings can't have doors there.
Trim Strips
Four narrow 3 mm strips with an etched centre fold line. Score along the etch, fold 90°, and glue 1.5 mm to each face that meets at the corner — hides the exposed cladding edges where two walls join.
Each F/B trim strip extends past the cladding by this amount on each end so it wraps to meet the side trim.
Inter-Floor Core Panels
Horizontal core-stock panels at each floor height. Panels have tongues on 3 sides; the 4th side rests against the wall installed last.
The wall you'll attach last during assembly. This wall has no slots for inter-floor tongues — the panels' open edges rest against its inner face when you close up the building.
Rooftop Mechanical Room
A small penthouse on the roof for HVAC, elevator overrun, water tanks, or stairwell access. Tongue-and-slot connection to the main roof.
Negative X = west, positive X = east. Negative Y = front, positive Y = back. Auto-clamped to fit on roof.
Rooftop Shield Wall
A low parapet wall around the rooftop equipment area — common on Japanese commercial buildings to hide AC units and tanks from street level.
X-braced structural cores (1.5 mm) with corner tongue-and-slot joinery and louvered cladding (0.28 mm) that glues on top. Drag handles in the floor editor to resize the outline, move it, add walk-through openings, or change per-wall length.
Default position only — once you drag the outline in the floor editor, that takes over.
Diagonal strip width. Smaller = more delicate brace; 0.5–0.8 mm looks right for most walls.
Billboards
Rooftop billboard structures. Each is a laser-cut assembly that glues to the roof.
No billboards yet — click Add to place one.
Laser Settings
Materials
Name each material. These names become subfolder names in the ZIP download. Assign each cladding style to a material so parts are grouped correctly.
